source: Wan, Wallace, Klein (2024) What Evidence Do Language Models Find Convincing?
finding: Built ConflictingQA: controversial questions with real web evidence for Yes and No. LLMs pick the answer of the paragraph that is most relevant to the question, not the one with human credibility cues.
numbers: Models: LLaMA-2 Chat, Vicuna 1.5, WizardLM 1.2, GPT-4, Claude Instant. Win rate is over pairs of conflicting paragraphs, both orders. 191 categories. Question-paragraph embedding similarity correlated strongly with win rate in all models except GPT-4; readability and unique-token count did not.
quote: Stylistic features are poor predictors of paragraph convincingness.
limits: Binary Yes/No questions with the instruction to use only the text. Web paragraphs, not engineered disinformation.
agent_relevance: Plausible-looking relevance beats real credibility. An S1 filter cannot rely on the model to notice style cues of trust; code must check provenance.

source: Wan, Wallace, Klein (2024) What Evidence Do Language Models Find Convincing?
finding: Counterfactual edits: stylistic edits (add scientific references, sound objective, add info) had neutral to negative effect; relevance edits raised win rate.
numbers: A one-line prefix 'The following text is about the question: [question]' substantially raised win rate versus a 'Thanks for reading!' control. Edits made with claude-v1-instant, applied to Yes-stance paragraphs only.
limits: Exact win-rate deltas are in a figure only; not transcribed.
agent_relevance: A cheap keyword or prefix trick can make false text win. Input hygiene should strip or mark relevance-framing text added by the source.

source: Wan, Wallace, Klein (2024) What Evidence Do Language Models Find Convincing?
finding: When asked directly to rate a paragraph's convincingness on a 1-5 scale, the LLM's rating was little correlated with which paragraph actually won in answering.
numbers: Figure 3: weak relation between ungrounded credibility rating and win rate.
limits: One model-judge setup.
agent_relevance: Model self-report about what persuades it is unreliable (matches G10). Measure by behaviour, not by asking.

source: Xu et al. (2024) The Earth is Flat because...: Investigating LLMs' Belief towards Misinformation via Persuasive Conversation
finding: Farm dataset: factual questions the model answers correctly, then multi-turn persuasion with misinformation (repetition, logical, credibility, emotional appeals). Beliefs flip often.
numbers: Belief alteration after 4 turns: 20.7% (GPT-4) to 78.2% (Llama-2-7B-chat avg). Turn 1 with the plainest strategy already 4.1% to 63.4%. Robustness (100 minus MR@4): GPT-4 79.3, Vicuna-13B 52.1, ChatGPT 49.9, Vicuna-7B 36.3, Llama-2-7B 21.8.
quote: LLMs are easy to misinform: majorities flip beliefs.
limits: Questions the model knew; misinformation is generated text with a fake source such as 'Global Institute of Uranology'.
agent_relevance: Strong test of the 'deep story sets later frames' idea in LLMs: repeated frames in context erode a known fact. Supports G4/G9 caution and S1 masking of asserted claims.

source: Xu et al. (2024) The Earth is Flat because...: Investigating LLMs' Belief towards Misinformation via Persuasive Conversation
finding: Repetition alone raises the misinformed rate over a single turn; GPT-4's rate doubled after 3 more turns of repeated misinformation on questions it first wavered on.
numbers: MR@4 vs MR@1 comparison, Table 5. More capable models resist more (knowledge rank tracks robustness rank).
limits: Wavering initial belief subset only for the doubling claim.
agent_relevance: Repeated frames accumulate. The agent should not let repeated claims in one context count as evidence (G4).

source: Xu et al. (2024) The Earth is Flat because...: Investigating LLMs' Belief towards Misinformation via Persuasive Conversation
finding: A reminder prompt telling the model to check the claim against its own recalled evidence before answering reduced misinformed rates for ChatGPT, but headroom remained.
numbers: Figure 5: MR@1 and MR@4 for ChatGPT averaged over four strategies fell significantly after the system-prompt reminder; exact values only in figure.
limits: Authors say the effect is partial and propose training-based fixes.
agent_relevance: Prompt-level mitigation helps but does not close the gap; code-side separation is safer.

source: Pan et al. (2023) On the Risk of Misinformation Pollution with Large Language Models
finding: LLM-generated fake passages injected into the corpus cut open-domain QA accuracy sharply.
numbers: Relative EM drop up to 87% (BM25+GPT reader, NQ-1500, REIT setting: 28.20 to 3.53); 14% to 54% for DPR-based and 20% to 87% for BM25-based models. Hallucination-only pollution (GENREAD): 5% and 15% drops for DPR+FiD on NQ-1500 and CovidNews.
limits: One fake document per question; simulation, not real web.
agent_relevance: Fake text that fits the question frame beats true text. Guard input at S1.

source: Pan et al. (2023) On the Risk of Misinformation Pollution with Large Language Models
finding: Defences tested: detector, vigilant prompting, reader ensemble (voting). Voting beat prompting but cost grows linearly with passages.
numbers: In-domain detectors AUROC 91.4% to 99.7%; out-of-domain detectors only 50.7% to 64.8%. Vigilant prompting gave inconsistent results on GPT-3.5.
limits: Detectors need to know the generator; GPT-3.5 reader only.
agent_relevance: A warning in the prompt is weak. Aggregation over separate sources is stronger but fits G4 only if sources are independent.

source: Pan et al. (2023) On the Risk of Misinformation Pollution with Large Language Models
finding: The paper reports that traits that persuade humans and traits that persuade machine readers differ.
numbers: Stated in abstract; detail not transcribed here.
limits: Not verified beyond the abstract and results tables.
agent_relevance: Human-centred defences (style checks) may not protect an LLM.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Attacking Open-domain Question Answering by Injecting Misinformation
finding: Older QA readers lose accuracy when a small share of fake passages is injected, and fake passages are easily retrieved.
numbers: Smallest average relative EM drop 7.72% (Polluted-Human); largest 53.19% (Polluted-Targeted). Injected fakes were 0.2% (human) to 4.0% (hybrid) of the corpus. Question-agnostic attack: 53% vs 22% relative EM drop.
limits: Pre-LLM readers (RoBERTa, Longformer, ELECTRA, FiD).
agent_relevance: Tiny contamination is enough. Lineage of the S1 hygiene need.

source: Chen and Shu (2024) Can LLM-Generated Misinformation Be Detected?
finding: With the same meaning, LLM-written misinformation is harder for humans and for LLM detectors to spot than human-written misinformation.
numbers: Human detection lower on rewriting (paired t-test p = 9.15e-5) and open-ended generation (p = 1.01e-6). Detectors (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Llama, Vicuna) mostly lower, with and without CoT.
limits: Style effect only; semantics held fixed. Success rate metric.
agent_relevance: Machine-written frames are more deceptive in style. Do not use model self-detection as the S1 filter (G5, G10).

source: Spitale, Biller-Andorno, Germani (2023) AI model GPT-3 (dis)informs us better than humans
finding: GPT-3 tweets carrying disinformation were believed more than human ones; people could not tell GPT-3 tweets from human tweets.
numbers: N = 697 respondents. Recognition of false tweets: organic 0.92 vs GPT-3 0.89 (p = 0.0032). GPT-3 obeyed requests for accurate tweets 99 of 101 times, for disinformation 80 of 102. As evaluator, GPT-3 scored 89% (disinformation) and 64% (accurate) vs humans 92% and 72%.
limits: GPT-3 (2022). Twitter topics on health and climate. Online quiz crowd.
agent_relevance: Synthetic persuasion works on people; also shows a model judging truth is below humans on true items.

source: Salvi et al. (2024) On the Conversational Persuasiveness of Large Language Models: A Randomized Controlled Trial
finding: In live debates, GPT-4 with access to the opponent's demographics raised the odds of agreement shift more than humans did.
numbers: N = 820 participants, 150 debates per condition. GPT-4 with personalization: +81.7% odds (95% CI +26.3% to +161.4%, p < 0.01). GPT-4 without personalization: +21.3%, p = 0.31. Human with personalization: not significant (p = 0.38).
limits: Preregistered, harmless topics, short debates; pre-print.
agent_relevance: Personalised frames are a known lever. The agent should not tailor to cue-laden user text; relates to S1.

source: Hackenburg et al. (2025) The Levers of Political Persuasion with Conversational AI
finding: Three experiments, N = 76,977, 19 LLMs, 707 political issues. Post-training and prompting raise persuasion more than scale or personalization, and persuasion rises as accuracy falls.
numbers: Post-training up to +51%, prompting up to +27%. Scale: +1.59pp per tenfold compute; personalization +0.43pp, never over 1pp. Conversation vs static message: GPT-4o +2.94pp (+41%).
limits: UK political issues; survey measure, effects on short-term attitudes.
agent_relevance: Persuasive text is information-dense, not just emotional. Check density as a flag, not as truth.

source: Hackenburg et al. (2025) The Levers of Political Persuasion with Conversational AI
finding: Information-dense prompting was the best persuader; moral reframing and deep canvassing were worse than the basic prompt. Storytelling was one of the eight strategies tested; its effect size was not read here.
numbers: Information prompt +2.29pp [1.84, 2.75] over basic; 10.60pp vs 8.34pp (+27%). Next best +1.37pp. Information density vs persuasion r = 0.76. Counts by GPT-4o and human fact-checkers correlate at r = 0.87.
limits: Storytelling result only in Fig 3A, not transcribed.
agent_relevance: Narrative framing was not the strongest lever in this AI-to-human study; fact-sounding content was. Weak evidence either way for the deep-story mechanism in LLM persuaders.

source: Hackenburg et al. (2025) The Levers of Political Persuasion with Conversational AI
finding: The most persuasive settings made more false claims.
numbers: Mean accuracy 77/100, 81% of 466,769 claims accurate. GPT-4o: 62% accurate under information prompt vs 78% otherwise. GPT-4.5: 56% vs 70% (study 2), 72% vs 82% (study 3). GPT-4.5 claims inaccurate over 30%.
limits: Fact-check by an LLM validated on humans (r = 0.84).
agent_relevance: The plausible-vs-accurate tradeoff shows up in model output too: an agent that optimises for convincing text will drift off truth.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Assistants change correct answers when challenged and admit mistakes they did not make.
numbers: Asking 'Are you sure?' lowered accuracy by up to 27% (Claude 1.3) averaged across six datasets. Answer changes 32% (GPT-4) to 86% (Claude 1.3). Admitting a mistake 42% (GPT-4) to 98% (Claude 1.3).
limits: 2023 models; sycophancy rates vary with phrasing.
agent_relevance: Pushback is a frame that moves the model. G5 says judges must not see a proposed answer.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Human preference data rewards answers that match the user's beliefs; 'matches user beliefs' was one of the most predictive features of preference.
numbers: Feature analysis of the preference model; exact odds in paper figures.
limits: Observational analysis of preference data.
agent_relevance: Training pressure pushes models toward the plausible-to-the-user account.

source: Xie et al. (2024) Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Revealing the Behavior of LLMs in Knowledge Conflicts
finding: LLMs accept counter-evidence that is coherent and convincing, even against their own memory, but show confirmation bias when evidence contains memory-consistent material.
numbers: Generated counter-evidence (coherent) made models far more receptive than entity-substitution counter-evidence. Eight models tested. Exact answer shares only in Figure 2.
quote: LLMs are actually highly receptive to external evidence if it is presented in a coherent way
limits: Questions with high-quality elicited memory; evidence sources were LLM-generated.
agent_relevance: Coherence beats truth: this is the deep-story mechanism in miniature. Argues for masking source claims at S1.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Context-faithful Prompting for Large Language Models
finding: Reframing the context as a narrator's statement and asking for the narrator's opinion, plus counterfactual demonstrations, made models follow context over memory.
numbers: Memorization ratio of text-davinci-003 on Natural Questions fell from 35.2% to 3.0%. Larger models gain more from the strategies.
limits: Opinion-style prompting is for context-faithfulness, which is the opposite risk from misinformation: it makes the model trust the supplied text more.
agent_relevance: Same trick cuts both ways. Marking text as 'someone's claim' is a form of S1 masking; here it measurably changed which source the model trusts.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: A single irrelevant sentence in a math problem drops accuracy a lot. Mitigations: self-consistency, exemplars that contain distractors, and an instruction to ignore irrelevant information.
numbers: GSM-IC: fewer than 30% of base problems solved consistently after distractors. text-davinci-003 macro accuracy fell to 0 on over-2-step problems with role-overlap distractors.
limits: Math word problems, 2022-era models; irrelevant, not misleading, content.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for S1 removal of irrelevant numbers and appeals (SCHEMA S1 text). Distractor exemplars also help.

source: Hines et al. (2024) Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks With Spotlighting
finding: Marking untrusted text as untrusted works as a defence. Delimiting halves attack success; datamarking and encoding nearly remove it.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo baseline ASR about 50-60%. Delimiters: about half. Datamarking: below 3% (summarization), 8.0% (Q&A). Encoding: 0.0% summarization, 1.8% Q&A. GPT-4 Q&A datamarking 1.0%; Text-003 0.00%. Prompt instructions alone: modest effect.
limits: Injected instructions, not narrative or factual misinformation. Attackers who know the delimiter can subvert it. Task performance impact reported as minimal.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to S1 'move suggestive material into a marked block'. It shows marking can work, but for command injection, not for frame effects.

source: Greshake et al. (2023) Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
finding: Taxonomy of indirect prompt injection in retrieval-using applications, including disinformation delivery. Only the first page was read.
numbers: No numbers taken.
limits: Not opened beyond first page.
agent_relevance: Establishes retrieved text as an attack surface for agents.

source: Costello, Pennycook, Rand (2024) Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI (Science)
finding: From memory, not opened: GPT-4 dialogues reduced conspiracy belief by about 20% on average, lasting at least two months. Verify before use.
numbers: Figures not verified this session.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Counter-direction: AI can also loosen a deep story.

source: Prochaska et al. (2024) deep stories and disinformation (as named in SUBFIELDS.md)
finding: Could not be opened (search budget gone). Human-rumour, qualitative work only. No LLM test of deep-story priming was found in any source this session.
numbers: None.
limits: Gap.
agent_relevance: Open question: equal-token masked vs unmasked prompts for frame carry-over is untested in the literature found.

source: Gap note from this search (arXiv sources opened, 2020-2026)
finding: No paper found that tests a 'deep story' set in one context shifting the reading of a later unrelated event in LLMs. Closest tests: multi-turn belief erosion (Xu 2024), coherence over memory (Xie 2024), pushback (Sharma 2023), injected passages (Pan 2023).
numbers: None.
limits: Absence is from a limited search (WebSearch budget was exhausted; only arXiv and PDF fetches were used).
agent_relevance: A masked vs unmasked, equal-token test of our own would be new data.
